title: Redemption of Preference Shares
outcomes: Explain why companies issue redeemable preference shares and what redemption means.
State the provisions of section 55 and the role of the capital redemption reserve.
Journalise redemption out of a fresh issue, out of divisible profits and by a combination, including premium on redemption and sale of investments.
Compute the minimum fresh issue needed to comply with section 55 and to provide funds.
Deal with partly called-up and fully called but partly paid preference shares before redemption.
Prepare the balance sheet after redemption.

meta.exam_tip: Remember three rules: CRR = nominal value redeemed − face value of fresh issue; premium on redemption comes out of profits; only fully paid shares are redeemed.

concepts.title: What redemption means
body: Redemption is the repayment of preference share capital at a pre-agreed amount and time. The redemption date (maturity) is usually printed on the share certificate. Holders receive dividends while the shares are outstanding and their capital back on redemption.
Redemption also lets a company reshape its capital structure — for example, replacing costly preference capital with equity or other securities when that suits its growth.
Since the Companies Act, 2013 prohibits irredeemable preference shares, every preference share must eventually be redeemed (normally within 20 years).
concepts.analogy: Like a fixed-term rental agreement with a date on which the deposit must be returned.
concepts.work: Finance teams keep a redemption calendar and plan funding (fresh issue, profits, sale of investments) months ahead of each due date.

concepts.title: Purpose of issuing redeemable preference shares
body: They are a practical way to raise finance when the primary market is dull.
Investors may hesitate to buy shares of a company whose shares are not traded; knowing the company will buy them back makes them easier to sell.
The company can redeem them when it has surplus capital that it cannot use profitably.
Unlike interest on debentures or loans, preference dividend need not be paid in a loss year — it is an appropriation of profit, not a charge against profit.
concepts.analogy: A "return-guaranteed" ticket: easier to sell because the buyer knows when the money comes back.
concepts.work: Start-ups and family companies often use redeemable preference shares in funding rounds; CAs model the redemption cash outflow in projections.

concepts.title: Section 55 — the legal conditions
body: A company limited by shares, if its articles allow, may issue preference shares redeemable within 20 years of issue (longer only for notified infrastructure projects).

(a) Redemption only out of divisible profits (profits otherwise available for dividend) or out of money raised by a fresh share issue made specially for this. (b) Only fully paid shares can be redeemed.

(c) Premium on redemption: companies of the prescribed class whose statements follow the accounting standards under s. 133 must provide it out of profits before redemption (for shares issued before the Act, out of profits or securities premium); other companies may use profits or securities premium. This unit, like the study material, assumes companies follow s. 133 standards — so premium is written off out of profits.

(d) Where shares are redeemed out of profits, an amount equal to the nominal value redeemed is transferred from divisible profits to Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR). CRR is treated like paid-up share capital for reduction of capital, and may be used only for fully paid bonus shares.
concepts.analogy: Section 55 is the rule that if you take a brick out of the wall (capital), you must put another brick in — either a new brick (fresh issue) or one made from your own savings (CRR).
concepts.work: Auditors verify every redemption against s. 55: fully paid status, source of funds, CRR transfer and premium treatment. A shortfall in CRR is a reportable non-compliance.

concepts.title: Why the capital "gap" must be filled — and the CRR
body: Creditors and lenders rely on the company's capital as a cushion. Redemption pays capital out, so s. 55 requires the gap to be filled by (a) proceeds of a fresh issue of shares, (b) capitalisation of undistributed profits through CRR, or (c) a mix of both.

With a fresh issue, both capital and assets are replaced directly. With profits, the replacement is indirect: profits that could have gone out as dividend are locked in CRR and kept in the business; since CRR can only become bonus shares, those profits ultimately turn into share capital.

Only divisible profits (general reserve, surplus in profit and loss, other revenue reserves available for dividend) can be used for CRR. Capital reserve, securities premium, revaluation reserve and existing CRR cannot.
concepts.analogy: CRR is a locked locker inside the company: profits moved there can never be taken home as dividend.
concepts.work: When reviewing reserves, a CA tags each one as divisible or not — the same tagging is used for dividend declaration, bonus issue and redemption.

concepts.title: Method 1 — redemption out of a fresh issue of shares
body: New equity or preference shares can be issued; their proceeds replace the redeemed capital. Debenture proceeds cannot be used, since debentures are borrowings.
If the fresh issue is at a premium, only the face value counts as "proceeds" for replacing capital; the premium is credited to securities premium and can be used only for s. 52 purposes.

Reasons to issue fresh equity: the capital is needed permanently (and equity carries no fixed dividend); profits available for dividend are insufficient; liquidity is weak. Advantages: no net cash outflow; new shares may command a premium; shareholders keep an equity interest. Disadvantages: future earnings are diluted; shareholding pattern changes if outsiders subscribe (a rights issue avoids this).
Entries: Bank Dr, To Share Capital (To Securities Premium); Preference Share Capital Dr (and Premium on Redemption Dr), To Preference Shareholders; Preference Shareholders Dr, To Bank.
concepts.analogy: Refinancing a home loan: take a new loan to repay the old one — the house (capital base) is unchanged.
concepts.work: In practice, the fresh issue and the redemption are timed so the new money arrives before the payout date.

concepts.title: Method 2 and combinations — profits, minimum fresh issue, sale of investments
body: Out of profits: Divisible profits Dr, To CRR (nominal value redeemed). Advantages: equity percentages unchanged; surplus funds used. Disadvantage: liquidity falls, and assets such as investments may need to be sold.
Combination: CRR = nominal value redeemed − face value of fresh issue.

Minimum fresh issue (s. 55 test): (1) find the maximum divisible profits available (after amounts the board wants retained and after providing the redemption premium out of profits); (2) minimum proceeds = nominal value redeemed − that amount; (3) minimum shares = minimum proceeds ÷ face value of one share; (4) round up to the next whole share or required multiple.

Funds test: shortfall = amount payable − cash available (bank + sale of investments); shares = shortfall ÷ issue price (face value + premium); issue the higher of the two tests. Profit or loss on sale of investments goes to the statement of profit and loss.
concepts.analogy: Two separate locks: the "law lock" (s. 55 capital replacement) and the "cash lock" (enough money to pay). The fresh issue must open both.
concepts.work: Treasury and secretarial teams run exactly these two tests when proposing a redemption plan to the board.

concepts.title: Partly called-up and partly paid preference shares
body: Only fully paid shares can be redeemed. If shares are partly called up and the question says they are to be redeemed, assume the final call is made and collected first.
If both fully paid and partly paid preference shares exist and nothing is said, redeem only the fully paid shares and leave the partly paid ones.

Fully called but partly paid (calls in arrears): if arrears are collected (Bank Dr, To Calls in Arrears) the shares become fully paid and are redeemed normally. If not paid despite notice, the shares may be forfeited: Preference Share Capital Dr (called up), To Calls in Arrears, To Forfeited Shares. Being due for redemption, they are not re-issued; the number redeemed falls and Forfeited Shares is transferred to Capital Reserve.
concepts.analogy: You can only return a full deposit — if someone has not finished paying theirs, they must pay up first or lose what they paid.
concepts.work: Before a redemption, the registrar's list of partly paid holders is checked; reminder and forfeiture notices are issued as per the articles.

jobs.title: Redemption plan for a board meeting
jobs.role: Company secretary and finance controller of an unlisted company
jobs.situation: Preference shares of ₹5 crore fall due in three months at a 5% premium. Free reserves are ₹3.2 crore; the board wants to keep at least ₹1 crore. Cash is tight.
steps: Premium ₹25 lakh to be met out of profits — reserve available for CRR = 3.2 − 1 − 0.25 = ₹1.95 crore.
Minimum face value of fresh issue = 5 − 1.95 = ₹3.05 crore.
Compare with cash shortfall and issue price to find the funds requirement; take the higher.
Check the shares are fully paid; plan final calls or forfeiture if any are not.
Draft resolutions for the fresh issue and for the CRR transfer.
jobs.takeaway: A good redemption note shows the law test, the cash test and the reserve impact on one page.

jobs.title: Audit check: was the CRR right?
jobs.situation: A client redeemed ₹40 lakh preference shares, financed by issuing equity of face value ₹15 lakh at a premium of ₹10 lakh. It transferred ₹15 lakh to CRR, arguing that the fresh issue brought in ₹25 lakh.
steps: Recall: only the face value of the fresh issue counts; premium is ignored.
Propose: General Reserve Dr ₹10 lakh, To CRR ₹10 lakh; check divisible profits are available.
Report non-compliance if the client refuses.
jobs.takeaway: Premium on a fresh issue never reduces the CRR requirement.

mcqs.q: Preference shares can be redeemed only if they are:
mcqs.explain: Section 55(2)(a) of the Companies Act, 2013 allows redemption only of fully paid preference shares. Partly paid shares must first be made fully paid (by calls) before they can be redeemed. The trap 'cumulative' describes the dividend right, which has nothing to do with eligibility for redemption. In practice: before a redemption date, the company secretary checks that all calls on the preference shares have been received.

mcqs.q: Which of the following can be used for redemption of preference shares?
options: Proceeds of a fresh issue of equity shares
Proceeds of an issue of debentures
mcqs.explain: Section 55 allows redemption only out of divisible profits or the proceeds of a fresh issue of shares made for that purpose. A fresh equity issue therefore qualifies. The trap 'proceeds of debentures' is wrong — debentures are borrowings, and replacing share capital with debt would weaken creditors' protection. Revaluation and capital reserves are not divisible profits. In practice: companies often refinance redeemable preference shares with a fresh equity issue or a rights issue.
mcqs.topic: Methods of Redemption of Fully Paid-up Shares

mcqs.q: Preference shares of ₹6,00,000 are redeemed out of a fresh issue of equity of face value ₹2,00,000 issued at a 20% premium, and the rest out of profits. Transfer to CRR is:
mcqs.explain: CRR = nominal value of shares redeemed − face value of the fresh issue = 6,00,000 − 2,00,000 = ₹4,00,000. The premium on the fresh issue (20% of 2,00,000 = ₹40,000) is ignored because only face value replaces capital. The trap ₹3,60,000 deducts the issue proceeds including premium. In practice: auditors verify the CRR transfer, since capital lost on redemption must be replaced either by new capital or by locking up profits.
mcqs.topic: Methods of Redemption of Fully Paid-up Shares

mcqs.q: Capital redemption reserve can be used for:
mcqs.explain: Section 55 says the capital redemption reserve may be applied only in paying up unissued shares to be issued as fully paid bonus shares. It cannot pay dividends, write off expenses or pay calls on partly paid shares. The trap 'paying up partly paid shares' is allowed only from free reserves. In practice: companies with a large CRR often use it later for a bonus issue to existing shareholders.

mcqs.q: For a company following the accounting standards under s. 133, premium on redemption of preference shares is provided out of:
mcqs.explain: For companies following the accounting standards prescribed under section 133, section 55(2)(d)(i) requires the premium on redemption to be provided out of profits before the shares are redeemed. Securities premium cannot be used for this by such companies — that is the trap. In practice: a company planning a redemption at a premium sets aside the premium from its profits well before the due date.

mcqs.q: Which reserve is a divisible profit for creating CRR?
mcqs.explain: Divisible profits are profits available for dividend. General reserve is a revenue reserve built from profits, so it can be transferred to CRR. Securities premium, capital reserve and revaluation reserve are not available for dividend, so they cannot be used. The trap 'securities premium' looks like a reserve but is capital in nature. In practice: companies use general reserve or retained earnings for the CRR transfer on redemption.

mcqs.q: Preference shares of ₹5,00,000 are to be redeemed. Divisible profits available ₹3,00,000. Minimum number of equity shares of ₹10 each to be issued at ₹10 to comply with s. 55:
mcqs.explain: Section 55 requires the nominal value redeemed to be covered by divisible profits or by a fresh issue. Gap = 5,00,000 − 3,00,000 = ₹2,00,000, which must be raised by fresh shares at face value. Shares at ₹10 = 2,00,000 ÷ 10 = 20,000. The trap 50,000 ignores the available profits; 30,000 confuses profits with the shortfall. In practice: CAs compute this minimum issue first, then check whether it also gives enough cash.
mcqs.topic: Methods of Redemption of Fully Paid-up Shares

mcqs.q: The minimum face value to be raised by a fresh issue is ₹2,05,005. Shares of ₹10 each must be issued in multiples of 50. The minimum number of shares is:
mcqs.explain: Minimum face value needed = ₹2,05,005. Shares needed = 2,05,005 ÷ 10 = 20,500.5, rounded up to 20,501 whole shares. Since shares must be in multiples of 50, the next multiple is 20,550. The trap 20,500 rounds down and leaves a shortfall; 20,501 ignores the multiple-of-50 rule. In practice: companies set issue lots such as multiples of 50 or 100 for administrative convenience.
mcqs.topic: Methods of Redemption of Fully Paid-up Shares

mcqs.q: Amount payable on redemption ₹7,20,000; bank ₹1,20,000; investments sold for ₹1,80,000. Equity shares issued at ₹15 (face value ₹10). Minimum shares to provide funds:
mcqs.explain: Cash needed = ₹7,20,000. Available = bank 1,20,000 + investments sold 1,80,000 = ₹3,00,000. Shortfall = ₹4,20,000. Each new share brings ₹15 (face value plus premium), so shares needed = 4,20,000 ÷ 15 = 28,000. The trap 42,000 divides by face value ₹10, ignoring the premium received in cash. In practice: treasury teams plan redemptions by listing every source of cash before deciding the size of a fresh issue.
mcqs.topic: Methods of Redemption of Fully Paid-up Shares

mcqs.q: Investments costing ₹3,00,000 are sold for ₹2,70,000 to fund redemption. The loss of ₹30,000 is:
options: Debited to the statement of profit and loss
Added to the cost of redemption
mcqs.explain: Loss on sale of investments is a revenue item, debited to the statement of profit and loss. It does not affect the redemption amount, CRR or securities premium. The trap 'debited to CRR' wrongly uses a reserve that can be applied only for bonus shares. In practice: companies selling investments to fund redemptions report any profit or loss on sale in the profit and loss statement for that year.
mcqs.topic: Methods of Redemption of Fully Paid-up Shares

mcqs.q: A company has both fully paid and partly paid redeemable preference shares and the question is silent. It should:
options: Redeem only the fully paid shares
Redeem all shares at their paid-up value
Redeem the partly paid shares first
mcqs.explain: Only fully paid preference shares can be redeemed under section 55. When a company has both fully paid and partly paid shares and the question is silent, it redeems only the fully paid ones; partly paid shares remain until they are made fully paid. The trap 'redeem all at paid-up value' is not allowed under section 55. In practice: before redemption, a company calls the unpaid amount on partly paid shares or forfeits shares if calls are not met.
mcqs.topic: Redemption of Fully Called But Partly Paid-up Preference Shares

mcqs.q: 2,000 preference shares of ₹100 (fully called, ₹75 paid) are forfeited before redemption. The amount transferred to capital reserve is:
mcqs.explain: Shares that are fully called but only ₹75 paid are forfeited for non-payment. The amount received, ₹75 × 2,000 = ₹1,50,000, is credited to forfeited shares. Since forfeited preference shares are cancelled rather than re-issued, this is transferred to capital reserve. The trap ₹50,000 is the unpaid call. In practice: forfeiture before redemption removes defaulting holders, and their paid amount becomes a capital reserve.
mcqs.topic: Redemption of Fully Called But Partly Paid-up Preference Shares

mcqs.q: Preference shares must ordinarily be redeemed within:
mcqs.explain: Section 55 requires preference shares to be redeemable within 20 years of issue. Companies engaged in notified infrastructure projects may issue preference shares for longer than 20 years (up to 30 years), subject to redeeming a minimum 10% each year from the 21st year. The trap 'ten years' is too short. In practice: infrastructure companies financing long-gestation projects often use this extended redemption window.

questions.q: State the provisions of section 55 of the Companies Act, 2013 relating to the redemption of preference shares.

items: A company limited by shares may, if authorised by its articles, issue preference shares redeemable within 20 years of issue (longer only for notified infrastructure projects); irredeemable preference shares are not allowed.
Redemption only out of profits otherwise available for dividend, or out of money raised by a fresh share issue made specially for this.
Only fully paid shares can be redeemed.
Premium on redemption: for prescribed companies following s. 133 accounting standards, out of profits before redemption; for other companies, out of profits or securities premium.

Where redeemed out of profits, a sum equal to the nominal value redeemed is transferred to Capital Redemption Reserve; CRR is treated as paid-up capital for reduction purposes and can be used only for fully paid bonus shares.

viva.q: State the main conditions of section 55 for redemption of preference shares.
viva.model: Preference shares must be redeemable within twenty years from issue, except for notified infrastructure projects. Shares can be redeemed only out of divisible profits or out of money raised by a fresh share issue made for that purpose. Only fully paid shares can be redeemed. When shares are redeemed out of profits, a sum equal to their nominal value must be transferred to the capital redemption reserve. Any premium on redemption must be provided out of profits, or for companies not covered by the prescribed accounting standards, out of profits or securities premium, before redemption.

viva.q: Why is a capital redemption reserve created, and for what can it be used?
viva.model: When preference shares are redeemed out of profits, the capital that leaves the company must be replaced, so that the funds available to protect creditors are not reduced. An amount equal to the nominal value redeemed out of profits is moved from divisible profits to the capital redemption reserve, which then cannot be paid as dividend and is treated like paid-up capital for reduction purposes. Its only permitted use is issuing fully paid bonus shares.

points.pt: Replaces redeemed capital so creditors' security is not reduced

viva.q: In deciding the transfer to CRR, why is the premium on a fresh issue ignored, and can debenture proceeds be used?
viva.model: Section 55 counts only the proceeds of a fresh issue of shares, and only the face value part replaces the capital redeemed. Securities premium can be applied only for the purposes allowed by section 52, so premium on the fresh issue is not treated as proceeds for replacing capital. Proceeds of debentures cannot be used either, because debentures are borrowings, not share capital.

viva.q: How do you calculate the minimum number of fresh shares to be issued for redemption?
viva.model: First find the maximum divisible profits available for redemption, after any amount the board wants to retain and after providing the premium on redemption out of profits. Minimum proceeds needed equals the nominal value of preference shares redeemed minus those available profits. Divide it by the face value of one new share and round up to the next whole share or the required multiple. Separately, if funds are short, divide the shortfall in cash by the full issue price including premium, and issue the larger number.

Divide by the face value of one new share (premium excluded)
Round up to next whole share / multiple
Funds test: shortfall ÷ issue price; take the higher

viva.q: How are partly called or partly paid preference shares dealt with on redemption?
viva.model: Only fully paid shares can be redeemed. If shares are partly called up, the company first makes the final call and collects it before redemption; if both fully paid and partly paid shares exist and nothing is said, only the fully paid shares are redeemed. If calls are in arrears, the company either collects the arrears or forfeits the shares after notice. Forfeited shares are not re-issued; they are cancelled, the number redeemed falls, and the forfeited amount goes to capital reserve.

viva.q: Why might a company issue redeemable preference shares?
viva.model: They help raise money when the primary market is dull, and investors are more willing to invest in an unlisted company if they know the shares will be bought back. The company can repay them when it has surplus funds it cannot use profitably. Also, dividend need not be paid in a loss year, unlike debenture interest, because preference dividend is an appropriation of profit and not a charge.

cases.title: Navya Pharma Ltd — planning a redemption
cases.case: Navya Pharma Ltd (a company following the notified accounting standards) must redeem 60,000 9% preference shares of ₹10 each at a premium of 10% on 31 March 2027. It has a general reserve of ₹4,00,000, of which the board wants to keep at least ₹1,00,000, a surplus in profit and loss of ₹60,000 and securities premium of ₹50,000. The premium on redemption is to be met from the surplus. Bank balance is ₹3,30,000. It will issue equity shares of ₹10 each at ₹15.

mcqs.q: Out of which balance must the premium on redemption be provided?
mcqs.explain: Navya follows the notified accounting standards, so section 55(2)(d)(i) requires the premium on redemption to be provided out of profits before redemption. Here the surplus in profit and loss is used. The trap 'securities premium' is not allowed for such companies. In practice: CAs check that the premium on redemption is charged to profits, not reserves like securities premium.

mcqs.q: What is the minimum number of equity shares to satisfy section 55?
mcqs.explain: Nominal value redeemed = 60,000 × ₹10 = ₹6,00,000. Divisible profits available for CRR: general reserve 4,00,000 − 1,00,000 kept = ₹3,00,000 (the whole surplus of ₹60,000 is used for the 10% premium). Minimum fresh issue at face value = 6,00,000 − 3,00,000 = ₹3,00,000 → 30,000 shares of ₹10. The trap 20,000 divides the gap by issue price ₹15. In practice: the company issues at least this many shares to satisfy section 55.
mcqs.topic: Methods of Redemption of Fully Paid-up Shares

mcqs.q: Is that issue enough for funds? Cash needed is the redemption amount; cash available is bank plus issue proceeds. What is the bank balance after paying the shareholders?
mcqs.explain: Amount payable = 6,00,000 + 10% premium 60,000 = ₹6,60,000. Cash available = bank 3,30,000 + 30,000 shares × ₹15 = 3,30,000 + 4,50,000 = ₹7,80,000. Balance after payment = 7,80,000 − 6,60,000 = ₹1,20,000, so the issue gives enough funds. The trap ₹3,30,000 is just the opening bank balance, ignoring both the issue and the payment. In practice: CAs check both the legal minimum issue and the cash requirement before finalising the issue size.
mcqs.topic: Methods of Redemption of Fully Paid-up Shares

mcqs.q: What amount is transferred to capital redemption reserve?
mcqs.explain: CRR = nominal value redeemed − face value of fresh issue = 6,00,000 − 3,00,000 = ₹3,00,000, transferred from general reserve. The premium on the fresh issue is ignored for CRR. The trap ₹6,00,000 ignores the fresh issue; ₹1,50,000 deducts the full issue proceeds of ₹4,50,000, including premium. In practice: the CRR protects creditors by keeping capital intact after preference shares are repaid.

summary: Redemption = repayment of preference capital; irredeemable preference shares are not allowed; normally within 20 years.
Section 55: only fully paid shares; out of divisible profits or fresh issue of shares; CRR = nominal value redeemed out of profits; premium on redemption out of profits (s. 133 companies).
CRR = nominal value redeemed − face value of fresh issue; usable only for bonus shares.
Minimum fresh issue: (nominal redeemed − available divisible profits) ÷ face value; funds test: shortfall ÷ issue price; take the higher, round up.
Partly called: make final call first. Arrears unpaid: forfeit, cancel, forfeited amount → capital reserve.
remember: Premium on a fresh issue is not "proceeds" for CRR.
Debenture proceeds can never fund redemption under s. 55.
Profit/loss on sale of investments goes to P&L.

Dividing the s. 55 shortfall by the issue price.
